finding: The API has no usable machine-readable contract. 3 of ~6,738 properties are marked required; no length, format or pattern metadata exists; 4 error codes are documented across 1,306 endpoints; 1 of the measured response shapes is documented.
business_impact: Validation depth is capped by documentation, not by test effort. No amount of automation work can assert a rule nobody has written down, so a large fraction of the API can only ever be smoke-tested. Defects in validation logic ship undetected because there is no stated correct behaviour to compare against.
risk: Invalid data accepted into a privileged-access product without detection. Integration consumers cannot build correct clients.
action_item: Publish an OpenAPI specification covering all 1,306 endpoints with required/length/format/pattern per property, plus an error-code registry with meanings.
recommendation: Treat the specification as a deliverable with an owner and a date, not documentation debt. Generate it from the source annotations so it cannot drift, and gate it in CI.
dependency: Requires developer access to the controllers serving the 96.3% of endpoints absent from the pam/PAM repo.

finding: Only 48 of 1,306 endpoints (3.7%) exist in the PAM developer repository supplied for analysis. The source of the remaining ~96% has not been provided.
business_impact: QA cannot derive request contracts, validation rules or error semantics independently. Every gap becomes a developer question, and the analysis stalls at the speed of those answers.
risk: Testing remains permanently reactive and incomplete. QA cannot give an evidence-based release opinion on the majority of the API.
action_item: Identify and grant access to the source tree that actually serves the API under test, or supply the generated contract in its place.
recommendation: Confirm which repository and branch build the QA API at u16hf, then either grant read access or commit to publishing the generated spec per build.
dependency: MF-01 is largely satisfied by this being resolved.

finding: Two ActivityLogs endpoints stop the IIS application pool. Three sequential ordinary requests took the entire API to HTTP 503 with no self-recovery. This was not a load test.
business_impact: A single client making three routine calls can take the product's whole API surface down. LH-08 puts 98 endpoints at risk.
risk: Availability incident in any environment, triggerable accidentally by an integration partner or a monitoring probe. In production this is a customer-visible outage.
action_item: Fix the hang in GetErrorLogs / GetLogs / GetAllActiveUserDetails and add a request timeout plus pool-level protection.
recommendation: Treat as a production availability defect rather than a test-environment quirk. Automation cannot validate it - re-execution is forbidden - so the fix must be verified by development with the capture in ISSUE-010.

finding: The shared GenericScheduler service account is locked, and it is simultaneously the automation API account and the data-warehouse ETL account.
business_impact: A test-side lockout became a data-warehouse outage. Automation currently depends on a human manually issuing a 24-hour token before every run, which makes unattended CI execution impossible.
risk: Recurring ETL outages caused by test activity; no scheduled regression capability.
action_item: Provision a dedicated, non-shared automation service account with a long-lived credential or a documented programmatic token flow.
recommendation: Separate the accounts first - that removes the blast radius immediately - then address the token lifetime. Also unlock GenericScheduler for ETL.
dependency: Blocks any unattended or scheduled API regression run.

finding: The framework asserted essentially HTTP status only. Negative testing covered 401/404/405 across 3 controllers; positive testing did not check schema, mandatory fields, business rules, persistence or audit. On an API where rejections return HTTP 200, a status assertion can pass against a rejected request.
business_impact: Green suites were not evidence of correct behaviour. A measured run illustrates the gap precisely: 90% of calls returned HTTP 200 while the true pass rate across all layers was 64%.
risk: False confidence at release. Defects the suite was believed to cover were never actually asserted.
action_item: Adopt the new twelve-layer validation package and migrate the existing API suites onto it.
recommendation: Delivered this objective: PamEnvelope, PamApiValidator, ValidationReport, ErrorCodeRegistry, DbPersistenceValidator. Migration of the 71 positive and 5 negative suites is the remaining work and is QA-side, needing no developer dependency.
dependency: Layers L9/L10 remain NOT_RUN until MF-01 supplies mandatory-field and business-rule metadata.

finding: Database validation had never run and could not have. AutoConfigs read two DB properties from key names present in no environment file, db_type was hardcoded to mysql while the URL was SQL Server, and DBUtils had zero callers and returned no consumable data.
business_impact: Nothing in the framework ever confirmed that an API-reported write reached the database - the one check that would have caught a Success:true response that wrote nothing.
action_item: None outstanding on the framework: fixed and verified end to end against QA this objective.
recommendation: Replace the supplied sysadmin login with a least-privilege QA-scoped account before persistence checks are wired into CI. See MF-08.
dependency: Full value depends on MF-07 - confirming the API's actual write target.

finding: RESOLVED, and the resolution reverses this finding. It originally claimed the QA API might not write to the supplied database, based on 'no row newer than 2025-10-01 on the server'. That was a sampling error - one column checked in the wrong databases. The newest timestamp in ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA is 2026-08-03 15:29:18, minutes old, and row counts rose during the investigation. The API's writes land there, confirmed three independent ways: the audit log names created objects in plaintext (runner IP 10.10.1.242, sal_Api_user_id=2), business tables hold them stamped created_by='SYSTEM_API', and ArconPamApiLog holds 194 rows from the runner across 62 methods.
business_impact: Database validation is possible and immediately productive - and it is now the only thing that can settle what the API-side run left open, since for 101 of 107 read-backs the API evidence cannot separate 'never created' from 'created but not readable back'. Column encryption turned out to be narrow (three table families), and the plaintext audit log routes around it.
risk: Residual risk is only that persistence assertions are enabled while the login is still sysadmin - see MF-08.
action_item: None on the write target. Proceed to enable L11 persistence assertions once the least-privilege account (MF-08) is in place.
recommendation: Retained rather than deleted so the reasoning error and its correction are both traceable. The approach, per-type feasibility and embeddable SQL are in docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md.
dependency: MF-08 gates enabling it in CI.

finding: Three security defects found in the QA database during the feasibility study. (1) At-rest encryption is deterministic - one key, no IV, functionally AES-ECB: sso_services holds 20,651 rows but only 59 distinct ss_port ciphertexts, one covering 91% of rows, and an identical ciphertext appears across 3 columns in 2 tables. (2) sso_ApiUsers stores passwords in cleartext, and tbl_KeyEncryptionDecryption holds an unencrypted private key in the same database it protects. (3) 16,560 of 313,197 rows in ssR_Users_Services (5.3%) grant access to services that no longer exist, deletion does not cascade, and only 5 foreign keys exist across 552 tables.
business_impact: In a privileged-access-management product these are the defect classes the product exists to prevent. Deterministic encryption leaks plaintext by frequency analysis with no key at all. Cleartext credentials plus a co-located private key mean read access to the database is read access to everything. Dangling authorisation rows are stale access grants.
risk: Direct security exposure, and a credibility risk: a PAM product storing credentials in cleartext is difficult to defend to a customer or an auditor.
action_item: Escalate all three to security review. Randomise the IV per row; move credentials to a hashed or vaulted store; relocate the encryption key out of the database it protects; add cascade or cleanup for authorisation rows.
recommendation: Raise separately from the QA findings - these are product security defects, not test observations, and they were found incidentally. Note that fixing the deterministic encryption will break ciphertext-equality lookups, which is why the framework validates by primary key instead and does not depend on the defect.

finding: The database credential supplied for QA validation is sysadmin and dbcreator on a server hosting 30 databases, several of them not QA, and it is committed in plaintext to the environment file alongside every other credential in all 20 environment files.
business_impact: An automated test suite holds unrestricted authority over non-QA data, and the credential is in version control.
risk: Unrecoverable data loss from a single mistaken statement; credential disclosure through repository access.
action_item: Issue a least-privilege login scoped to ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA with SELECT only, and move all credentials out of version control into a secret store or CI-injected variables.
recommendation: Code-level mitigation is already in place - DBUtils refuses non-SELECT statements unless mutation is explicitly enabled, and requests driver-level read-only. That is a guard, not a substitute for correct permissions.
status: Mitigated in code - account and secret handling outstanding

finding: Chain-dependent testing collapses at the first hop. 196 hops failed to extract a new identifier, and only 2 of 107 created objects could be read back through the API. Only 13 of 217 create endpoints can be driven at all.
business_impact: End-to-end and multi-step workflows - the scenarios that reflect real product use - cannot be automated. Coverage is therefore concentrated on reads, which are the lowest-risk operations.
risk: The write paths of a privileged-access product are the least tested part of it.
action_item: Supply valid request bodies for the 217 create endpoints, or the metadata from which they can be generated.
recommendation: This is the highest-leverage single unblock available: it converts read-only coverage into genuine lifecycle coverage. It is the same root cause as MF-01 expressed at the execution layer.

finding: Two latent defects will bite as soon as the suite scales: APIExcelReportUtil mutates a static row index with no synchronisation under parallel='classes', and ApiHelper creates a Playwright instance per request without closing it.
business_impact: Report rows can overwrite each other, and a full-catalogue run leaks resources across 1,300+ requests. Both are harmless at today's test counts and both are directly in the path of the full negative matrix this objective specifies.
risk: Corrupted evidence and unstable runs precisely when coverage is scaled up - the worst possible moment to lose trust in the reports.
action_item: Synchronise the report row index and close Playwright instances per request.
recommendation: Fix before executing any suite over the full endpoint catalogue. Small, self-contained, no developer dependency.

finding: The bearer token committed to QA_MsSQL.properties expired 2026-07-31, and tokens are valid for 24 hours.
business_impact: Any suite trusting the committed token authenticates as nobody, and its failures will be misread as product defects.
action_item: Remove the committed token; read it from an environment variable at run time.
recommendation: A committed 24-hour credential is wrong on both counts - it is a secret in version control and it is stale within a day. Depends on MF-04 for a durable fix.

finding: The negative API test suite is largely non-functional, and the functional part tests the opposite of what it claims. 199 of 279 @DataProvider names referenced by the 386 negative test classes do not exist, so 650 @Test methods fail at TestNG initialisation. All 80 providers that do resolve read the POSITIVE data sheets - so a class named MissingParameter submits a complete valid payload. Separately, the 3,652-row negative workbook is declared in AutoConfigs and set in 6 environment files but read by no provider at all.
business_impact: Negative-testing coverage that appears to exist in the repository does not run, and where it runs it asserts the wrong thing. Any past statement of negative coverage based on this suite was not correct.
risk: The most severe category of false confidence: a test named for a defect class that would pass even if the product had no validation whatsoever.
action_item: Re-point every negative class at negative data, create the 199 missing providers or delete the tests referencing them, and either wire the negative workbook to a provider or remove it.
recommendation: Triage in three passes - delete what is dead, re-point what is mis-wired, then add assertions using the new validation package. Do not report negative coverage from this suite until pass two is complete. No developer dependency for any of it.
dependency: Assertion depth then depends on MF-01 for expected outcomes.

finding: Evidence now indicates the repository supplied is not merely incomplete but the wrong one. Twelve validation-constraint families return zero occurrences across all 6,866 .cs files, including Newtonsoft's Required.Always - yet the server demonstrably runs that exact check, with 123 rejections of that form observed live. All 3 [Required] attributes in the entire product sit on one class in a Provisioning service that is not among the 70 controllers under test, and their property names appear in 0 of 5,940 endpoint-mapped properties.
business_impact: Sharpens MF-02 from a coverage gap into a sourcing error. The validation logic exists and is running in production; it is simply in code QA has never been given. Time spent analysing pam/PAM for request contracts is time spent on the wrong artifact.
risk: Continued analysis of the wrong source produces confident but wrong conclusions - the most expensive kind of QA output.
action_item: Identify the microservices or projects holding the enforcing request models and grant read access, or publish their generated schemas.
recommendation: Ask one specific question rather than a general one: which project defines the request models for the ~1,258 endpoints absent from pam/PAM? A single answer unblocks MF-01, MF-09 and most of MF-12's assertion depth.
dependency: Supersedes the framing of MF-02; same owner.

finding: 73.4% of a complete negative test design cannot be judged, and 98.7% of endpoints have no runnable negative coverage today. Of 10,448 generated scenarios across all 1,306 endpoints, 7,664 have no documented expected outcome; only 172 (1.6%) carry a measured one. At property level, 98.9% of the derived scenario space is unassertable - 20,469 of 20,700.
business_impact: The negative test design is complete and delivered; what is missing is the product's own statement of correct rejection behaviour. Effort is no longer the constraint - the contract is.
risk: A privileged-access product whose input validation is largely unverifiable by any external party, including its own QA function.
action_item: Publish expected rejection behaviour - status, error code, message - per endpoint, prioritising the 217 create endpoints.
recommendation: The 7,664 undocumented rows are an itemised, endpoint-level work list ready to hand to development - not a general complaint. Prioritise by controller usage and start with creates.

finding: The endpoint blocklist that prevents an API outage is enforced in documentation and in the Python harness but NOT in the Java framework the CI pipeline runs. The framework's positive test data holds 102 rows across 50 controllers targeting the blocklisted action names, all expecting HTTP 200. Two of them are the exact endpoints measured to stop the IIS application pool, and they sit in the data for ActivityLogs - the single API class activated by CICD_Suites/APISuite.xml and by a newly git-tracked root testng.xml that IDEs pick up by convention.
business_impact: Running the CI API suite, or a developer pressing Run on the project in an IDE, can take the entire QA API to HTTP 503 with no self-recovery. The control that has governed every manual and harness run since the defect was found does not exist inside the framework that actually executes in CI. It is currently protected only by the fact that nobody has run that suite.
risk: A self-inflicted availability incident in QA, indistinguishable at first sight from a product failure. The same pattern in a pre-production environment would be a customer-visible outage.
action_item: Add a name-based guard in ApiHelper that refuses to issue a request whose action name is blocklisted, failing the test with an explicit message. Correct AGENTS.md and the repo CLAUDE.md, both of which still state no root testng.xml exists. Decide whether the root testng.xml should exist at all.
recommendation: Guard on names, never verbs - and put the guard in code rather than in data, because removing the 102 rows leaves nothing to stop them being re-added. This is the clearest case in the project for a safety control living in the framework rather than in a document: the documented rule was followed faithfully for months by everyone who read it, and the one execution path that does not read it is the automated one.
status: Open - found during OBJ-008, guard not applied pending approval
